title: Cardiac Chambers & Valves
front clue: Right heart sits anterior; the tricuspid inserts slightly closer to the apex
core concept: The heart has four chambers. The right atrium receives the superior and inferior vena cava and the coronary sinus; the right ventricle is the most anterior chamber, lies directly behind the sternum, and is recognized by its moderator band, coarse trabeculations and the more apical septal insertion of the tricuspid valve. The left atrium is the most posterior chamber and receives four pulmonary veins. The left ventricle is bullet shaped, has smooth walls with two papillary muscles (anterolateral and posteromedial), and normally measures about 0.6 to 1.0 cm in wall thickness at end-diastole. The atrioventricular valves are the tricuspid (anterior, septal and posterior leaflets) and mitral (anterior and posterior leaflets, with scallops A1-A3 and P1-P3). Both are tethered by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles. The semilunar valves are the aortic (right, left and noncoronary cusps) and pulmonic valves, each with three cusps and no chordae. Normal tricuspid septal leaflet insertion is only a few millimeters more apical than the mitral.
why it matters: Echo identification depends on morphology, not position, because congenital and surgical hearts can be rearranged. The morphologic right ventricle always carries the tricuspid valve, the moderator band and the more apical AV valve insertion; the morphologic left ventricle carries the mitral valve. Trap: the most anterior structure in a parasternal long-axis view is the RV outflow tract, not the left ventricle. Remember that the mitral valve has no septal chordal attachments, which is why a septal attachment suggests a tricuspid valve or an AV canal defect. Excessive apical displacement of the tricuspid valve is the hallmark of Ebstein anomaly.
on the registry: Expect questions on which chamber is most anterior or posterior, which features identify the morphologic RV, and how many leaflets or cusps each valve has.
checkpoint: RV: most anterior, moderator band, apical tricuspid; LA: most posterior, four pulmonary veins

title: Coronary Artery Anatomy
front clue: Left main splits to LAD and circumflex; whoever gives the PDA is dominant
core concept: The coronary arteries arise from the sinuses of Valsalva just above the aortic valve. The left main coronary artery arises from the left coronary sinus and divides into the left anterior descending (LAD) and the left circumflex (LCx). The LAD runs in the anterior interventricular groove toward the apex, giving diagonal branches to the anterior wall and septal perforators to the anterior two thirds of the septum. The LCx runs in the left AV groove and gives obtuse marginal branches to the lateral wall. The right coronary artery (RCA) arises from the right coronary sinus, runs in the right AV groove, and supplies the RV free wall, the inferior wall, the inferior septum and, in most people, the AV node. Dominance is defined by which artery gives rise to the posterior descending artery (PDA): right dominance occurs in about 80 to 85 percent of people. The posteromedial papillary muscle usually depends on the single PDA supply, while the anterolateral muscle has dual LAD and LCx supply.
why it matters: Coronary anatomy is the bridge between a wall motion abnormality and a diagnosis. If you know which artery feeds which wall, you can predict the territory of an infarct and its likely complications. The papillary muscle detail is a favorite: posteromedial papillary rupture is more common because it has a single blood supply, usually from the RCA via the PDA. Trap: the noncoronary cusp is the posterior cusp adjacent to the interatrial septum; no coronary artery arises from it. Because coronaries fill in diastole, tachycardia and a very low aortic diastolic pressure, as in severe aortic regurgitation, both reduce myocardial perfusion.
on the registry: Expect questions on which artery supplies a wall, how dominance is defined, and why one papillary muscle is more vulnerable than the other.
checkpoint: PDA decides dominance; right dominant in about 80 to 85 percent

title: Cardiac Cycle & ECG Timing
front clue: Valves closed twice: isovolumic contraction after QRS, isovolumic relaxation after T
core concept: Each heartbeat has systolic and diastolic phases tied to the ECG. The P wave represents atrial depolarization and is followed by atrial contraction, which produces the mitral A wave. The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization; shortly after its onset the mitral valve closes, and the ventricle enters isovolumic contraction, when all four valves are closed and pressure rises without volume change. When LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure, the aortic valve opens and ejection begins. The T wave represents ventricular repolarization; near its end the aortic valve closes, marking end-systole. Isovolumic relaxation follows, again with all valves closed, normally lasting about 70 to 90 milliseconds. When LV pressure falls below LA pressure, the mitral valve opens and rapid early filling produces the E wave, followed by diastasis and then atrial contraction. End-diastole is timed at the onset of the QRS or the frame just after mitral closure, and end-systole at the smallest LV cavity or aortic valve closure.
why it matters: Correct timing underpins every measurement on the exam. LV internal dimensions, volumes and wall thickness are measured at end-diastole, at the onset of QRS, while LA size is measured at end-systole, when the atrium is largest. Trap: the atria are filling during ventricular systole, so atrial dimensions peak just before mitral opening. Isovolumic periods lengthen with impaired relaxation, which is why a prolonged IVRT signals early diastolic dysfunction. If a Doppler signal falls in the wrong phase relative to the ECG, for example a diastolic jet you believed was systolic, you have probably misidentified the valve or the flow.
on the registry: Expect questions that pair an ECG event with a valve event, define the isovolumic periods, or ask when to measure the LV and LA.
checkpoint: P then A wave; QRS then mitral closure; end of T then aortic closure

title: Normal Intracardiac Pressures
front clue: Right heart about 25 over 5; left heart about 120 over 10
core concept: Normal resting pressures are a useful framework for Doppler. Right atrial mean pressure is about 2 to 6 mmHg. The right ventricle is about 15 to 30 mmHg systolic and 2 to 8 mmHg end-diastolic. The pulmonary artery is about 15 to 30 mmHg systolic and 8 to 15 mmHg diastolic, with a mean usually below 20 mmHg. Left atrial pressure, estimated by pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, is about 4 to 12 mmHg. The left ventricle is about 100 to 140 mmHg systolic and 3 to 12 mmHg end-diastolic, and the aorta about 100 to 140 over 60 to 90 mmHg. In the absence of outflow obstruction, RV systolic pressure equals PA systolic pressure, and LV systolic pressure equals aortic systolic pressure. Echo estimates pressures by adding a measured gradient to a known or estimated pressure: RVSP equals the TR gradient plus RA pressure. The RA pressure is estimated from IVC diameter and inspiratory collapse.
why it matters: Pressures turn Doppler velocities into physiology. Every gradient is a pressure difference between two chambers, so if you know one chamber and the gradient, you can calculate the other. Trap: RVSP equals PASP only when there is no pulmonic stenosis or RVOT obstruction. Another trap is forgetting to add RA pressure; the TR gradient alone underestimates RVSP. Use the left-sided numbers to sanity check results: an LV to LA gradient from MR of about 100 mmHg corresponds to roughly 5 m/s, which is the expected MR velocity in a normotensive patient. A much lower MR velocity suggests low LV pressure or a very high LA pressure.
on the registry: Expect questions asking for normal ranges, which chamber pressure equals another, and how echo derives a pressure by adding a gradient.
checkpoint: RVSP = PASP unless something obstructs the RV outflow

title: Standard TTE Views & Windows
front clue: Parasternal, apical, subcostal, suprasternal: four windows, each with a purpose
core concept: Transthoracic echo uses four main windows. The parasternal window, at the left third or fourth intercostal space with the index mark toward the right shoulder, gives the parasternal long-axis view of the RVOT, septum, LV, LA, mitral and aortic valves and aortic root; rotating 90 degrees clockwise gives short-axis views at the aortic valve, mitral valve, papillary muscle and apical levels. The apical window, at the point of maximal impulse, gives the four-chamber view (inferoseptum and anterolateral wall), five-chamber view (adds the LVOT and aortic valve), two-chamber view (anterior and inferior walls) and three-chamber or apical long-axis view (anteroseptum and inferolateral wall). The subcostal window shows the four chambers, interatrial septum and IVC, and is often best in COPD or ventilated patients. The suprasternal notch shows the aortic arch, head and neck vessels and descending aorta for coarctation and dissection. The right parasternal window is used with a nonimaging CW probe to capture peak aortic stenosis velocity.
why it matters: Most exam questions in this area ask which view best shows a structure or which walls appear in a view. Learn the wall pairs: apical four-chamber shows inferoseptal and anterolateral, apical two-chamber shows anterior and inferior, apical long-axis shows anteroseptal and inferolateral. Trap: apical foreshortening makes the apex look thick and falsely shortens the LV, underestimating volume; a true apex is thin and stationary at the tip. The subcostal view is preferred for the interatrial septum because the beam strikes it perpendicularly, reducing false dropout. For AS, interrogate from several windows, because the highest velocity sets the grade.
on the registry: Expect questions on which view best displays a structure, which walls appear in each apical view, and transducer orientation for each window.
checkpoint: A4C: inferoseptal and anterolateral; A2C: anterior and inferior; A3C: anteroseptal and inferolateral

title: LV Size & Ejection Fraction
front clue: Biplane Simpson's beats Teichholz whenever walls move unevenly
core concept: LV linear dimensions are measured in the parasternal long-axis view at end-diastole, perpendicular to the long axis at the level of the mitral leaflet tips. ASE normal LV internal diameter in diastole is about 4.2 to 5.8 cm in men and 3.8 to 5.2 cm in women, with septal and posterior wall thickness about 0.6 to 1.0 cm in men and 0.6 to 0.9 cm in women. Fractional shortening, (LVIDd minus LVIDs) divided by LVIDd, is normally about 25 to 43 percent. The Teichholz formula converts a single linear dimension into volume by assuming an ellipsoid shape, so it fails with regional wall motion abnormalities or distorted geometry. The ASE recommended 2D method is the biplane method of disks (modified Simpson's rule), tracing the endocardium in apical four- and two-chamber views at end-diastole and end-systole. EF equals (EDV minus ESV) divided by EDV. Normal LVEF is about 52 to 72 percent in men and 54 to 74 percent in women; under about 52 percent is commonly considered abnormal.
why it matters: The core reasoning is geometry: any method that extrapolates from one line assumes a symmetric ventricle, which is exactly what an infarct destroys. When a question describes an apical aneurysm or regional WMA, choose biplane Simpson's or 3D over Teichholz or M-mode. Trap: foreshortened apical views undercount length and underestimate volume; contrast improves endocardial definition when two or more contiguous segments are not seen. Trap two: trace the compacted myocardium inner border, excluding papillary muscles and trabeculations from the wall. Off-axis M-mode cuts the LV obliquely and overestimates dimensions, so 2D-guided measurement is preferred.
on the registry: Expect questions on the ASE recommended EF method, why Teichholz fails, where and when linear dimensions are measured, and normal values.
checkpoint: Uneven walls, use disks: biplane Simpson's, not Teichholz

title: Stroke Volume & Cardiac Output
front clue: A cylinder of blood: LVOT area times LVOT VTI equals one beat
core concept: Doppler stroke volume treats flow through the LVOT as a cylinder. LVOT diameter is measured in a zoomed parasternal long-axis view in mid-systole, inner edge to inner edge, about 0.3 to 1.0 cm below the aortic valve. Cross-sectional area equals pi times radius squared, or 0.785 times diameter squared. LVOT velocity time integral (VTI) is obtained with pulsed wave Doppler in the apical five-chamber or three-chamber view, with the sample volume placed just proximal to the valve at the same level as the diameter, and traced around the modal velocity. Stroke volume equals CSA times VTI. A normal LVOT VTI is about 18 to 22 cm; values under about 15 cm suggest low stroke volume. Cardiac output equals stroke volume times heart rate, normally about 4 to 8 L/min, and cardiac index equals CO divided by body surface area, normally about 2.5 to 4.0 L/min/m2. Stroke volume index under 35 mL/m2 defines low flow in aortic stenosis.
why it matters: The biggest error source is the diameter, because it is squared: a 1 mm error in a 2.0 cm LVOT changes area by about 10 percent. Measure carefully, at the same level as the PW sample, and average several beats in atrial fibrillation. Trap: placing the PW sample too close to the valve picks up prestenotic acceleration and overestimates VTI. LVOT VTI alone is a powerful trend marker in shock and heart failure because the diameter does not change within a patient. In the absence of significant regurgitation, the same stroke volume passes every valve, which is the foundation of the continuity equation.
on the registry: Expect calculation questions for SV, CO and CI, and questions about where to measure LVOT diameter and place the PW sample.
checkpoint: SV = 0.785 x D squared x VTI; CO = SV x HR

title: Bernoulli Equation & RVSP
front clue: Four v squared turns velocity into pressure; add RA pressure for RVSP
core concept: The simplified Bernoulli equation states that the pressure gradient in mmHg equals 4 times the peak velocity squared in m/s. A 4 m/s jet therefore represents a 64 mmHg gradient. It assumes the proximal velocity is negligible; when proximal velocity exceeds about 1.5 m/s, as in combined LVOT and valve obstruction or coarctation, the expanded form 4(V2 squared minus V1 squared) is preferred. RV systolic pressure is estimated as 4 times peak TR velocity squared plus right atrial pressure. RA pressure is estimated from the IVC: diameter 2.1 cm or less with more than 50 percent collapse on sniff suggests about 3 mmHg; diameter over 2.1 cm with less than 50 percent collapse suggests about 15 mmHg; other combinations suggest about 8 mmHg. A peak TR velocity above 2.8 m/s is a commonly used marker of possible pulmonary hypertension. PA end-diastolic pressure can be estimated from the end-diastolic PR velocity, 4V squared plus RA pressure, and mean PA pressure from the early peak PR velocity.
why it matters: Velocity is squared, so small errors become large gradient errors, and an angle of more than about 20 degrees significantly underestimates velocity. Doppler always underestimates if misaligned, never overestimates, so the highest clean velocity from multiple windows wins. Trap: a weak or incomplete TR envelope underestimates RVSP, and agitated saline or contrast can enhance it. Trap two: in severe free TR, the RA and RV equalize and the low TR velocity does not reflect true PA pressure. Bernoulli peak instantaneous gradients from echo are higher than the peak-to-peak gradients reported in older catheter labs, which explains apparent discrepancies.
on the registry: Expect calculations of gradient from velocity and RVSP from TR velocity plus an IVC-derived RA pressure.
checkpoint: Gradient = 4V squared; RVSP = 4(TR V) squared + RAP

title: Continuity Equation & PISA
front clue: What flows in must flow out: area times velocity stays constant
core concept: The continuity equation is based on conservation of mass: flow proximal to an orifice equals flow through it. For aortic stenosis, AVA equals LVOT CSA times LVOT VTI divided by aortic valve VTI. The dimensionless index (DVI), LVOT VTI divided by AV VTI, avoids the diameter entirely; a DVI below 0.25 suggests severe native AS. The same principle works for mitral stenosis and prosthetic valves, provided the reference site has no significant regurgitation. PISA (proximal isovelocity surface area) applies continuity to the hemispheric shell of converging flow proximal to a regurgitant orifice. Shift the color baseline toward the jet to lower the aliasing velocity to about 30 to 40 cm/s, then measure the radius from the first aliasing boundary to the orifice. Flow rate equals 2 pi r squared times aliasing velocity. EROA equals flow rate divided by peak regurgitant velocity, and regurgitant volume equals EROA times the regurgitant VTI. For MR, EROA of 0.40 cm2 or more and regurgitant volume of 60 mL or more indicate severe disease.
why it matters: Both equations compare a known area and velocity with an unknown one, so set them up as ratios before calculating. In PISA, the radius is squared, so a small radius error becomes a large EROA error; zoom on the orifice and measure in mid-systole. Trap: PISA assumes a hemisphere, which fails with a flat or very eccentric orifice and overestimates when the orifice lies on a constraining wall. Trap two: continuity using a mitral reference is invalid if there is significant MR. If the LVOT diameter seems unreliable, the DVI provides a diameter-free check on AS severity.
on the registry: Expect AVA calculations, DVI interpretation and PISA steps including why baseline shift is used and how EROA is derived.
checkpoint: A1 x V1 = A2 x V2; PISA flow = 2 pi r squared x Va

title: Diastolic Function
front clue: Four clues: e', average E/e', TR velocity, LA volume index
core concept: Diastolic assessment combines mitral inflow, tissue Doppler and chamber size. Mitral inflow PW is sampled at the leaflet tips in the apical four-chamber view, measuring E and A velocities, E/A ratio and E deceleration time. Tissue Doppler e' is measured at the septal and lateral annulus. In patients with normal EF, the 2016 ASE/EACVI guideline uses four variables: septal e' below 7 cm/s or lateral e' below 10 cm/s, average E/e' above 14, LA volume index above 34 mL/m2, and peak TR velocity above 2.8 m/s. If more than half are abnormal, diastolic dysfunction is present; if half are abnormal, the study is indeterminate. Grade I (impaired relaxation) shows E/A 0.8 or less with a small E and normal LA pressure. Grade II (pseudonormal) shows E/A between 0.8 and 2 with elevated filling pressure, unmasked by reduced e', high E/e' or a Valsalva-induced E/A decrease of 50 percent or more. Grade III (restrictive) shows E/A of 2 or more and short deceleration time under about 160 ms.
why it matters: The trap is pseudonormalization: a grade II inflow looks just like a normal one, so you must look at e', E/e', LA size and TR velocity before calling it normal. LA volume index works as the hemoglobin A1c of diastolic function, reflecting chronic filling pressure, while E/e' reflects the moment. Also remember that normal young adults can have E/A above 2 with normal e', which is not restrictive. Atrial fibrillation removes the A wave, and mitral annular calcification, prosthetic mitral valves and significant MR distort e' and E/e', making the algorithm unreliable.
on the registry: Expect questions on the four ASE variables and cutoffs, grading by E/A and deceleration time, and how to unmask pseudonormal filling.
checkpoint: Pseudonormal looks normal; e' and E/e' tell the truth

title: Aortic Stenosis Grading
front clue: Severe AS: 4, 40, 1.0: velocity, mean gradient, valve area
core concept: Calcific degenerative disease of a trileaflet valve is the most common cause of AS in older adults; bicuspid and rheumatic valves are the other major causes. 2D shows thickened, calcified, restricted cusps, often with concentric LV hypertrophy. ASE/AHA grading: mild AS has a peak velocity of 2.0 to 2.9 m/s, mean gradient under 20 mmHg and AVA over 1.5 cm2. Moderate AS has 3.0 to 3.9 m/s, 20 to 39 mmHg and 1.0 to 1.5 cm2. Severe AS has a peak velocity of 4.0 m/s or more, mean gradient of 40 mmHg or more, AVA under 1.0 cm2, indexed AVA under 0.6 cm2/m2 and DVI under 0.25. Peak velocity should be sought with CW Doppler from the apical, right parasternal, suprasternal and subcostal windows, often with a dedicated nonimaging probe. Classical low-flow, low-gradient AS has AVA under 1.0 cm2, mean gradient under 40 mmHg and reduced EF; paradoxical low-flow AS has the same numbers with preserved EF and a stroke volume index under 35 mL/m2.
why it matters: When the numbers disagree, think about flow. A small valve area with a low gradient means either the measurement is wrong, often an underestimated LVOT diameter, or flow is low. Low-dose dobutamine stress separates true severe AS, in which the gradient rises and the area stays small, from pseudosevere AS, in which the area opens. Trap: high-flow states such as anemia, fever or coexisting AR raise velocity and can exaggerate severity. The shape of the CW envelope helps: severe AS peaks late and is rounded, while mild AS peaks early and is triangular. Never grade from one window.
on the registry: Expect grading questions from given velocities, gradients or areas, and questions about the multiwindow search and low-flow, low-gradient AS.
checkpoint: Severe AS: Vmax 4 m/s, mean gradient 40 mmHg, AVA under 1.0 cm2

title: Bicuspid Aortic Valve
front clue: Two cusps open like a fish mouth, and the aorta comes along for the ride
core concept: The bicuspid aortic valve is the most common congenital heart abnormality, present in about 1 to 2 percent of people, with male predominance. The most frequent pattern is fusion of the right and left coronary cusps, often with a raphe that can make the valve look trileaflet in diastole. The valve must therefore be judged in systole in the parasternal short-axis view, where the opening is elliptical, or fish mouth shaped, rather than triangular. In the long-axis view, the cusps dome in systole. On M-mode, the diastolic closure line is often eccentric rather than centered in the aortic root. Bicuspid valves develop stenosis earlier than trileaflet valves, often in the 40s to 60s, and can also regurgitate. Associations include ascending aortic dilation (bicuspid aortopathy), coarctation of the aorta, and Turner syndrome. Complications include endocarditis and, less commonly, aortic dissection. The aortic root and ascending aorta should be measured on every bicuspid study.
why it matters: The classic error is calling a valve trileaflet from a diastolic frame when a raphe mimics a third commissure. Count commissures during systolic opening. Systolic doming in the long axis is a strong clue even when the short axis is poor. Trap: an eccentric M-mode closure line suggests but does not prove a bicuspid valve. Because the aortopathy is part of the disease, not just a consequence of stenosis, the ascending aorta can dilate even with a well-functioning valve, and first-degree relatives are often screened. Always look for coarctation from the suprasternal notch in a young patient with a bicuspid valve.
on the registry: Expect questions on the most common fusion pattern, how to avoid raphe errors, systolic doming and associated lesions.
checkpoint: Judge cusps in systole; raphe fools you in diastole

title: Mitral Stenosis
front clue: Hockey stick leaflet, fish-mouth orifice, area equals 220 divided by PHT
core concept: Mitral stenosis is almost always rheumatic in origin; degenerative calcific MS from severe annular calcification is increasing in elderly patients. Rheumatic MS shows commissural fusion, leaflet tip thickening and diastolic doming of the anterior leaflet, the hockey stick appearance in parasternal long axis, with restricted posterior leaflet motion. In parasternal short axis at the leaflet tips, the orifice is fish mouth shaped and can be planimetered in mid-diastole; planimetry is the reference 2D method. The normal mitral valve area is about 4 to 6 cm2. Pressure half-time is the time for the peak gradient to fall by half, and MVA equals 220 divided by PHT. Severe MS is defined as MVA of 1.5 cm2 or less, usually with PHT of 150 ms or more; very severe is 1.0 cm2 or less. Mean gradient, often above 10 mmHg in severe MS, depends on heart rate and flow. On M-mode, the EF slope is reduced and the posterior leaflet moves anteriorly with the anterior leaflet.
why it matters: PHT is easy but has limits: it is unreliable immediately after balloon valvotomy, with significant AR, and with abnormal LV or LA compliance, so planimetry or continuity is used then. Trap: planimetry must be at the true leaflet tips; scanning too far toward the base gives a falsely large area. Mean gradient rises with tachycardia, so always report heart rate. Before percutaneous valvotomy, the Wilkins score grades leaflet mobility, thickening, calcification and subvalvular disease; a score above about 8 predicts a poorer result, and moderate or greater MR or LA appendage thrombus, best seen on TEE, are contraindications.
on the registry: Expect MVA from PHT calculations, severity cutoffs, causes of PHT error and the classic 2D and M-mode appearance.
checkpoint: MVA = 220 / PHT; severe at 1.5 cm2 or less
ai_review_note: corePiece (low): Current ACC/AHA staging does not use mean gradient to define severe MS; at normal heart rates severe MS typically has a mean gradient of about 5 to 10 mmHg, and over 10 mmHg is the older EAE/ASE severe cutoff.

title: Rheumatic Heart Disease
front clue: Strep throat years ago: fused commissures and thick, shortened chordae today
core concept: Rheumatic heart disease follows acute rheumatic fever, an immune reaction to group A streptococcal pharyngitis. It is still common in low-resource regions and in immigrants. The mitral valve is affected most often, followed by the aortic valve, and multivalve disease is common; tricuspid involvement occurs, while pulmonic involvement is rare. Hallmarks are commissural fusion, leaflet thickening that is most pronounced at the tips, and thickened, shortened, fused chordae. The mitral valve can be stenotic, regurgitant, or both; acute rheumatic carditis more often causes MR, while chronic disease leads to MS. Rheumatic aortic valve disease shows commissural fusion with a triangular, central systolic orifice and often combined AS and AR, usually alongside mitral disease. Rheumatic tricuspid stenosis is usually associated with mitral disease. The World Heart Federation criteria are used for echo screening in endemic areas. Chronic sequelae include LA enlargement, atrial fibrillation, thromboembolism and pulmonary hypertension.
why it matters: The diagnostic reasoning is pattern recognition: the commissures fuse first, which separates rheumatic disease from degenerative disease, where calcium starts at the annulus and leaflet bases and the commissures stay open. If aortic valve disease is rheumatic, the mitral valve is almost always involved too, so an isolated aortic lesion with a normal mitral valve points elsewhere. Trap: mitral annular calcification can restrict inflow but does not fuse commissures. Rheumatic valves are also substrates for infective endocarditis, and the subvalvular apparatus severity strongly influences whether balloon valvotomy is feasible.
on the registry: Expect questions on which valve is most often involved, the hallmark of commissural fusion, and how rheumatic and degenerative disease differ.
checkpoint: Rheumatic fuses commissures; degenerative calcifies the base

title: Pulmonic & Tricuspid Stenosis
front clue: Pulmonic stenosis is congenital and domes; tricuspid stenosis is rare and rheumatic or carcinoid
core concept: Pulmonic stenosis is nearly always congenital. Valvular PS shows a thickened, systolic doming valve, often with post-stenotic dilation of the main pulmonary artery, and RV hypertrophy in significant cases. A dysplastic, thick, non-doming valve suggests Noonan syndrome. PS is graded by CW Doppler peak velocity in the parasternal short-axis or subcostal view: mild under 3 m/s (peak gradient under 36 mmHg), moderate 3 to 4 m/s (36 to 64 mmHg), and severe over 4 m/s (over 64 mmHg). Subvalvular obstruction from infundibular hypertrophy produces a late-peaking dagger-shaped signal. Tricuspid stenosis is uncommon; causes include rheumatic disease, almost always with mitral involvement, carcinoid heart disease, and less often obstruction by tumors or devices. TS shows thickened, restricted, diastolic doming leaflets with RA and IVC enlargement. Because gradients are low, a mean gradient of 5 mmHg or more, PHT of 190 ms or more, and valve area of 1.0 cm2 or less indicate significant TS. Measure averaged over the respiratory cycle because inspiration increases right-sided flow.
why it matters: Right-sided stenosis is tested because the numbers differ from the left side. A mean tricuspid gradient of only 5 mmHg is significant, which is why low-gradient signals must not be dismissed. Trap: in PS, RVSP from TR no longer equals PA systolic pressure; subtract the PS gradient to estimate PA pressure. Carcinoid disease more often causes severe TR from thickened, retracted, fixed leaflets than pure stenosis, and it usually spares the left heart unless there is a right-to-left shunt or lung metastases. Differentiate valvular from infundibular obstruction by the envelope shape and PW mapping.
on the registry: Expect PS grading from velocity, the low tricuspid gradient threshold, Noonan and carcinoid associations, and the PS effect on RVSP.
checkpoint: PS severe over 4 m/s; TS significant at mean gradient 5 mmHg

title: Mitral Regurgitation
front clue: Vena contracta 0.7, EROA 0.40, volume 60: the severe MR triad
core concept: MR is classified as primary, from a structural leaflet or chordal problem such as prolapse, flail or endocarditis, or secondary (functional), from LV or LA dilation causing tethering and annular dilation with structurally normal leaflets. Carpentier types describe leaflet motion: type I normal, type II excessive, and type III restricted. Severity uses an integrated approach. Mild MR has a vena contracta under 0.3 cm, a small central jet, EROA under 0.20 cm2 and regurgitant volume under 30 mL. Severe MR has a vena contracta of 0.7 cm or more, EROA of 0.40 cm2 or more, regurgitant volume of 60 mL or more, regurgitant fraction of 50 percent or more, a large central jet over 50 percent of LA area or a wall-hugging eccentric jet, a dense triangular CW signal, a mitral E velocity above 1.2 m/s, and systolic flow reversal in the pulmonary veins. A dominant A wave inflow argues against severe MR. Chronic severe MR enlarges the LA and LV.
why it matters: Color jet area is the most misleading parameter because it depends on gain, Nyquist limit and jet direction. Eccentric jets hug the LA wall and look smaller than they are (Coanda effect), so rely on vena contracta, PISA and pulmonary vein flow. Trap: acute severe MR, such as papillary rupture, may show a normal-sized LA and LV and a brief, low-velocity jet because LA pressure rises abruptly. Trap two: functional MR is dynamic and changes with loading, so note blood pressure. The jet points away from a prolapsing leaflet and toward a restricted one.
on the registry: Expect questions on severe MR cutoffs, primary versus secondary MR, eccentric jet pitfalls and pulmonary vein systolic reversal.
checkpoint: Severe MR: VC 0.7 cm, EROA 0.40 cm2, RVol 60 mL, pulmonary vein reversal
