ai_review_note: corePiece (medium): 2017 ASE native valve regurgitation guideline defines a severe central MR jet as more than 50 percent of LA area (40 percent was the older 2003 cutoff).

title: Aortic Regurgitation
front clue: Short PHT, wide jet, holodiastolic reversal: the aorta is leaking back
core concept: AR results from cusp disease, such as bicuspid valve, rheumatic disease or endocarditis, or from aortic root dilation, as in Marfan syndrome, hypertension or dissection. Severity combines several parameters. Severe AR shows a jet width of 65 percent or more of LVOT diameter, a vena contracta over 0.6 cm, a CW pressure half-time under 200 ms, holodiastolic flow reversal in the proximal descending aorta with end-diastolic velocity above about 20 cm/s, holodiastolic reversal in the abdominal aorta, EROA of 0.30 cm2 or more, regurgitant volume of 60 mL or more and regurgitant fraction of 50 percent or more. Mild AR shows a jet width under 25 percent of LVOT, vena contracta under 0.3 cm and PHT over 500 ms. Chronic severe AR causes LV dilation from combined volume and pressure load. On M-mode, the AR jet can cause high-frequency fluttering of the anterior mitral leaflet. In acute severe AR, LV diastolic pressure rises rapidly, causing premature mitral closure.
why it matters: PHT reflects how fast the aortic and LV pressures equalize, so it depends on LV compliance and systemic resistance as well as AR severity. A stiff ventricle or vasodilation shortens PHT and can exaggerate severity; use flow reversal and vena contracta to confirm. Trap: brief early diastolic reversal in the descending aorta is normal; only holodiastolic reversal suggests significant AR. Trap two: anterior mitral fluttering on M-mode indicates AR but does not grade it. Acute severe AR, as in endocarditis or dissection, may present with a normal-size LV, a very short PHT and premature mitral valve closure, a surgical emergency.
on the registry: Expect questions on PHT cutoffs, which flow reversal pattern is significant, jet width ratios and M-mode signs of AR.
checkpoint: Severe AR: PHT under 200 ms, holodiastolic reversal, jet over 65 percent of LVOT

title: Tricuspid & Pulmonic Regurgitation
front clue: Hepatic vein systolic reversal flags severe TR; a short, dense PR jet flags severe PR
core concept: Trace TR is present in most normal people. Pathologic TR is usually secondary, caused by RV or annular dilation from pulmonary hypertension, left heart disease or atrial fibrillation, and less often primary, from endocarditis, carcinoid, Ebstein anomaly, rheumatic disease or pacemaker leads. Severe TR features include a vena contracta of 0.7 cm or more, a large central jet over about 10 cm2, EROA of 0.40 cm2 or more, regurgitant volume of 45 mL or more, systolic flow reversal in the hepatic veins, a dense triangular early-peaking CW signal, a dilated IVC and RA, and a tricuspid E velocity often above 1 m/s. In severe free TR, the RA and RV pressures equalize and the jet velocity may be low. Mild PR is a normal finding. Pathologic PR occurs with pulmonary hypertension, which produces a high-velocity jet, and after tetralogy repair or pulmonary valvotomy. Severe PR shows a wide jet filling the RVOT, a dense CW signal with steep deceleration ending before end-diastole, and RV dilation.
why it matters: TR velocity reflects pressure, not severity: a modest jet can be fast with pulmonary hypertension, and massive TR can be slow. Never grade TR by velocity. Hepatic vein systolic reversal is a specific sign of severe TR, but atrial fibrillation blunts systolic forward flow and can mimic it. Trap: in severe PR, laminar low-velocity flow can be missed with color because there is little turbulence; look for diastolic flow reversal in the branch pulmonary arteries and an early termination of the CW signal. Device leads can impinge on leaflets and cause TR, so assess lead interaction in 3D or multiple views.
on the registry: Expect questions on hepatic vein flow reversal, secondary TR mechanisms, the low-velocity jet of free TR and severe PR features.
checkpoint: Velocity tells pressure; hepatic veins tell TR severity

title: Mitral Valve Prolapse
front clue: More than 2 mm above the annulus in parasternal long axis, not the four-chamber view
core concept: Mitral valve prolapse is systolic displacement of one or both leaflets more than 2 mm above the mitral annular plane into the LA, measured in the parasternal long-axis or apical three-chamber view. It affects about 2 to 3 percent of the population. The four-chamber view should not be used to diagnose prolapse because the saddle-shaped annulus makes normal leaflets appear to bow above the plane. Classic prolapse includes leaflet thickening of 5 mm or more; nonclassic prolapse has thinner leaflets. Barlow disease is diffuse myxomatous degeneration with bulky, redundant leaflets and multisegment prolapse, while fibroelastic deficiency is thin leaflets with a localized prolapse, often P2, and chordal rupture. A flail leaflet occurs when chordal rupture lets the leaflet tip point into the LA. The MR jet is directed away from the prolapsing leaflet: posterior prolapse produces an anteriorly directed jet. On M-mode, prolapse shows a mid to late systolic posterior hammock motion. Clinically there is a mid-systolic click and late systolic murmur.
why it matters: The saddle shape is the key reasoning point; it is why prolapse was overdiagnosed historically, and why the exam asks which view to use. A flail leaflet is a step beyond prolapse: the tip points into the atrium rather than the body billowing. Trap: in prolapse, the jet direction is opposite to the affected leaflet, while in restricted motion the jet goes toward the affected leaflet. Prolapse is associated with Marfan syndrome and other connective tissue disorders, and with arrhythmias. Severe MR from flail leaflet is a strong surgical indication, so describe the segment involved.
on the registry: Expect questions on the 2 mm criterion, which view is avoided, jet direction relative to the affected leaflet and flail versus prolapse.
checkpoint: Prolapse jets point away from the bad leaflet

title: Infective Endocarditis
front clue: Vegetations sit on the upstream, low-pressure side of the valve
core concept: Infective endocarditis is infection of the endocardium, usually the valves, most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci. Vegetations are irregular, mobile, echogenic masses attached to the upstream, low-pressure side of a valve: the atrial surface of the mitral and tricuspid valves and the ventricular surface of the aortic and pulmonic valves. They typically show independent, chaotic motion and often prolapse into the downstream chamber. Risk factors include prior endocarditis, prosthetic valves, congenital and rheumatic disease, intravenous drug use, which favors the tricuspid valve, and indwelling devices. Echo evidence of vegetation, abscess, new prosthetic dehiscence or new regurgitation is a major modified Duke criterion. Complications include valve perforation and destruction with severe regurgitation, perivalvular abscess, especially of the aortic root, pseudoaneurysm, fistula, and embolization. Vegetations over 10 mm and highly mobile vegetations carry higher embolic risk. TTE is the first test, but TEE has much higher sensitivity and is indicated for prosthetic valves, suspected abscess, high clinical suspicion with a negative TTE, and device infection.
why it matters: Location rules come from flow: vegetations grow where the high-velocity jet strikes the low-pressure side. Use this to separate a vegetation from a mimic. Lambl excrescences are thin filaments on the closure line of aortic cusps, and nodules of Arantius are small central thickenings; neither moves chaotically. Trap: a negative TTE does not exclude endocarditis, especially on a prosthetic valve, where shadowing hides the atrial side of a mitral prosthesis. Perivalvular extension, such as an aortic root abscess, can produce new conduction block and is often a surgical indication. Marantic and Libman-Sacks lesions are sterile and are in the differential.
on the registry: Expect questions on vegetation location, IV drug use and the tricuspid valve, complications such as abscess and when to move to TEE.
checkpoint: Upstream side: atrial on AV valves, ventricular on semilunar valves

title: Prosthetic Valves
front clue: Mechanical lasts but clots; bioprosthetic avoids warfarin but wears out
core concept: Prosthetic valves are mechanical or biological. Mechanical types are bileaflet tilting disc, the most common, single tilting disc and caged ball. They require lifelong anticoagulation, cast strong shadows and reverberations, and normally have small closing and leakage washing jets. Biological valves include stented porcine or bovine pericardial valves, stentless valves, homografts and transcatheter valves; they need no long-term anticoagulation but degenerate, typically after about 10 to 15 years. Normal prosthetic aortic valves show a DVI of 0.30 or more and acceleration time under 80 ms; a DVI under 0.25 with acceleration time over 100 ms suggests obstruction. Normal mitral prostheses usually show peak E under 1.9 m/s, mean gradient of 5 mmHg or less and PHT under 130 ms. Patient-prosthesis mismatch is an indexed EOA that is too small for body size, severe below 0.65 cm2/m2 for aortic. Obstruction is caused by thrombus, often softer, larger and acute, or pannus, dense fibrous ingrowth. Dehiscence shows a rocking motion of the sewing ring with paravalvular regurgitation outside the ring.
why it matters: Always compare with the baseline postoperative study; prosthetic gradients vary by type and size, so a single number can mislead. High gradients can mean obstruction, mismatch, high flow or regurgitation, and DVI and acceleration time help sort them. Trap: bileaflet valves in small sizes show pressure recovery and localized high velocity through the central orifice, which overestimates gradients. Trap two: a mitral prosthesis shadows the LA on TTE, so MR is often underestimated; TEE is the definitive test. Paravalvular leaks occur outside the sewing ring and are common after transcatheter replacement.
on the registry: Expect questions on valve types, normal washing jets, DVI and acceleration time cutoffs, mismatch, thrombus versus pannus and dehiscence.
checkpoint: Prosthetic AV obstruction: DVI under 0.25, acceleration time over 100 ms

title: Dilated Cardiomyopathy & Heart Failure
front clue: Big, round, weak ventricle with a wide mitral E-point septal separation
core concept: Dilated cardiomyopathy is LV dilation with globally reduced systolic function not explained by coronary disease or abnormal loading. Causes include genetic disease, myocarditis, alcohol, chemotherapy such as anthracyclines, peripartum cardiomyopathy and tachycardia; ischemic cardiomyopathy produces a similar picture with regional scars. Echo shows an enlarged, spherical LV with thin or normal walls, global hypokinesis and a reduced EF. Secondary findings are functional MR from tethering and annular dilation, LA enlargement, elevated filling pressures, reduced LVOT VTI and possible LV apical thrombus. On M-mode, the E-point septal separation (EPSS) is increased, with values above about 7 mm suggesting reduced EF, and a B-bump on the mitral closure line indicates elevated LV end-diastolic pressure. Heart failure is classified by EF: reduced EF (HFrEF) is 40 percent or less, mildly reduced is 41 to 49 percent, and preserved EF (HFpEF) is 50 percent or more. Global longitudinal strain is a sensitive marker for subclinical dysfunction, especially in cardio-oncology, where a relative fall of more than about 15 percent is significant.
why it matters: The reasoning is that a dilated, weak LV pulls the papillary muscles apart, so MR in DCM is usually secondary and improves with therapy. EPSS increases because the poorly ejecting ventricle has a low stroke volume and the dilated cavity moves the septum away from the mitral leaflet; aortic regurgitation and mitral stenosis also widen EPSS, which is a trap. Global hypokinesis does not exclude coronary disease, so regional patterns matter. Always look at the apex with contrast if needed, because a low-flow apex is the classic site for thrombus. Serial EF and strain guide therapy, including defibrillator decisions.
on the registry: Expect questions on DCM appearance, M-mode EPSS and B-bump, heart failure EF categories and secondary MR mechanism.
checkpoint: HFrEF 40 percent or less; HFpEF 50 percent or more

title: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
front clue: Thick septum, SAM and a late-peaking dagger jet that grows with Valsalva
core concept: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is genetic LV hypertrophy, usually from sarcomere gene variants, not explained by loading conditions. The diagnosis requires wall thickness of 15 mm or more in any segment, or 13 mm or more with a family history or positive genetic test. The classic pattern is asymmetric septal hypertrophy with a septal to posterior wall ratio of about 1.3 or more; other forms include concentric, midventricular and apical (Yamaguchi) hypertrophy, which gives a spade-shaped cavity and may need contrast to see. Obstructive HCM shows systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral leaflet or chordae against the septum, creating dynamic LVOT obstruction, a posteriorly directed MR jet, and mid-systolic partial closure or notching of the aortic valve on M-mode. CW Doppler through the LVOT shows a late-peaking, dagger-shaped envelope. An LVOT gradient of 30 mmHg or more at rest or with provocation indicates obstruction, and 50 mmHg or more is the usual threshold for septal reduction therapy. Diastolic dysfunction, LA enlargement and reduced e' are typical.
why it matters: Obstruction is dynamic, so anything that decreases preload or afterload or increases contractility increases the gradient: Valsalva strain, standing, amyl nitrite, dehydration and dobutamine. Squatting, handgrip and leg raising decrease it. If the resting gradient is under 50 mmHg, provoke with Valsalva or exercise. Trap: the dagger-shaped late-peaking LVOT signal must not be confused with the MR jet, which starts earlier with isovolumic contraction and has a higher velocity, often over 5 to 6 m/s. Separate them by color guidance and timing. Athlete's heart shows milder, symmetric hypertrophy with normal or enhanced diastolic function and a normal or dilated cavity.
on the registry: Expect questions on wall thickness criteria, SAM and its M-mode signs, maneuvers that change the gradient and LVOT versus MR jet differentiation.
checkpoint: Valsalva makes the HCM gradient grow; squat makes it shrink

title: Restrictive Cardiomyopathy & Amyloidosis
front clue: Thick, sparkling walls, big atria and a cherry-on-top strain pattern
core concept: Restrictive cardiomyopathy is a stiff, noncompliant myocardium with high filling pressures, usually with normal or near-normal LV size and EF. Causes include cardiac amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, Fabry disease, endomyocardial fibrosis and radiation. Amyloidosis, either transthyretin (ATTR) or light chain (AL), is the classic exam example. Echo features include increased LV and RV wall thickness, a granular sparkling myocardial texture, biatrial enlargement, thickened valves and interatrial septum, a small pericardial effusion, and restrictive filling with E/A above 2, deceleration time under about 160 ms and markedly reduced e'. Longitudinal strain shows apical sparing, with relatively preserved apical strain and reduced basal and mid strain, the cherry-on-top bull's-eye pattern. The ECG paradoxically shows low voltage despite thick walls. Restrictive physiology is distinguished from constrictive pericarditis by reduced tissue Doppler e', no significant respiratory variation in mitral inflow and the absence of septal bounce. Cardiac MRI, nuclear scintigraphy and biopsy confirm the subtype.
why it matters: The key reasoning is that the myocardium is the problem in restriction, while the pericardium is the problem in constriction, so tissue velocity separates them: e' is low in restriction and preserved or high in constriction. Trap: sparkling texture is enhanced by harmonic imaging and is not specific, so rely on the full constellation. Thick walls with low ECG voltage strongly suggest infiltration, while hypertensive or hypertrophic hearts show high voltage. Amyloid also deposits in the atria, so atrial standstill and LA appendage thrombus can occur even in sinus rhythm.
on the registry: Expect questions on amyloid echo features, apical sparing strain, restrictive filling numbers and restrictive versus constrictive differentiation.
checkpoint: Restriction: low e'; constriction: preserved e'

title: Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy
front clue: Ballooning apex, hyperkinetic base, stress trigger and open coronaries
core concept: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, also called stress-induced or apical ballooning cardiomyopathy, is acute, usually reversible LV dysfunction triggered by emotional or physical stress, most often in postmenopausal women. It presents like an acute coronary syndrome with chest pain, ECG changes and modest troponin rise, but coronary angiography shows no culprit obstructive lesion. The classic echo pattern is akinesis or ballooning of the mid and apical segments with hyperkinesis of the basal segments, producing a shape like the Japanese octopus trap. Variants include reverse or basal Takotsubo, midventricular and focal forms. A key feature is that the wall motion abnormality extends beyond a single coronary territory, typically circumferentially. Complications include LVOT obstruction from basal hyperkinesis with SAM, mitral regurgitation, LV apical thrombus, cardiogenic shock, arrhythmias and, rarely, free wall rupture. RV involvement predicts a more complicated course. Function usually recovers within days to weeks, which confirms the diagnosis on follow-up echo.
why it matters: Think in territories. An LAD infarct can involve the apex, but Takotsubo involves the apex circumferentially, including inferior and lateral apical segments, beyond what one artery explains. Trap: a wraparound LAD can mimic this pattern, so angiography is still required. Recognizing LVOT obstruction is critical because inotropes such as dobutamine worsen it, while fluids and beta blockers can help. Always examine the akinetic apex for thrombus. Follow-up echo showing full recovery separates Takotsubo from infarction, in which a scarred segment remains abnormal.
on the registry: Expect questions on the classic ballooning pattern, demographics, nonobstructive coronaries, LVOT obstruction and reversibility.
checkpoint: Apex balloons, base squeezes, coronaries clean, function returns

title: RV Function & Pulmonary Hypertension
front clue: TAPSE under 17 mm, S' under 9.5 cm/s, FAC under 35 percent: the RV is failing
core concept: The RV is crescent shaped and wraps around the LV, so no single view captures its volume. ASE recommends a focused RV apical four-chamber view and several measures. RV dilation is suggested by a basal diameter above 41 mm. Systolic dysfunction is indicated by TAPSE (tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion, M-mode at the lateral annulus) under 17 mm, tissue Doppler S' under 9.5 cm/s, fractional area change under 35 percent. Pulmonary hypertension is now defined hemodynamically as a mean PA pressure above 20 mmHg. Echo estimates probability using peak TR velocity above 2.8 m/s and supporting signs: RV dilation, septal flattening, a PA diameter larger than the aortic root, PA acceleration time under about 100 ms or mid-systolic notching of the RVOT Doppler signal and a dilated, noncollapsing IVC. A D-shaped LV with septal flattening only in diastole suggests RV volume overload; flattening in systole and diastole suggests pressure overload. In acute pulmonary embolism, McConnell sign is RV free wall akinesis with preserved apical motion.
why it matters: TAPSE is easy and reproducible but measures only longitudinal function at one site and is angle dependent; after cardiac surgery TAPSE is often reduced because longitudinal motion falls after pericardiotomy, even when overall RV function is preserved. Use multiple parameters. Trap: septal flattening timing distinguishes volume from pressure load, a classic exam question. Trap two: an underestimated TR jet can hide pulmonary hypertension, so use supporting signs. McConnell sign suggests acute PE but is not specific; chronic thromboembolic disease shows a hypertrophied, dilated RV with higher TR velocity than acute PE can generate.
on the registry: Expect questions on TAPSE, S' and FAC cutoffs, septal flattening timing, McConnell sign and PH supporting findings.
checkpoint: Diastolic flattening: volume; systolic flattening: pressure

title: 17-Segment Model & Wall Motion Scoring
front clue: Six basal, six mid, four apical and one cap: score 1 to 4
core concept: The ASE and AHA 17-segment model divides the LV into six basal segments, six mid segments, four apical segments and the apical cap. Basal and mid levels each have anterior, anteroseptal, inferoseptal, inferior, inferolateral and anterolateral segments; the apical level has anterior, septal, inferior and lateral segments. The 17th segment, the apical cap, is the tip beyond the cavity and is mainly used for perfusion imaging and contrast studies; a 16-segment model is often used for wall motion. Each segment is scored by endocardial excursion and systolic wall thickening: 1 is normal or hyperkinetic, 2 is hypokinetic (reduced thickening), 3 is akinetic (thickening under about 10 percent), and 4 is dyskinetic (systolic outward motion). The wall motion score index is the sum of scores divided by the number of segments scored; a normal ventricle scores 1.0, and higher values reflect larger areas of dysfunction. Thin, bright, akinetic segments under about 6 mm thick suggest scar from prior infarction.
why it matters: Wall thickening is more reliable than endocardial motion because a passive segment can be pulled inward by its neighbors, called tethering, and the whole heart translates. Watch the thickening of each segment from the inside border. Trap: an abnormal septal motion after cardiac surgery, with left bundle branch block or with RV pacing, is not ischemia if thickening is preserved. Trap two: apical foreshortening hides apical abnormalities. Practice naming the segments seen in each view, because exam questions often describe a view and an abnormality and ask which segment or artery is involved.
on the registry: Expect questions on the number of segments per level, scoring definitions, the score index and thickening versus motion.
checkpoint: 1 normal, 2 hypokinetic, 3 akinetic, 4 dyskinetic

title: Coronary Territories
front clue: LAD front and septum; RCA the floor; circumflex the side
core concept: Coronary territories map coronary anatomy onto the 17 segments, recognizing normal variation. The LAD typically supplies the basal and mid anterior and anteroseptal segments and all apical segments except sometimes the apical inferior and lateral, plus the apical cap. In the apical four-chamber view, the LAD supplies the apical septum; in the two-chamber view, the anterior wall; and in the three-chamber view, the anteroseptum. The RCA, in a right-dominant system, supplies the basal and mid inferior and inferoseptal segments and often the apical inferior segment, plus the RV free wall. The LCx supplies the basal and mid anterolateral and inferolateral segments and often the apical lateral segment. Areas of overlap include the apical lateral and apical inferior segments, which can be supplied by the LAD, the RCA or the LCx. Inferolateral segments are most often supplied by the LCx but may come from the RCA. RV involvement with an inferior infarct indicates proximal RCA occlusion.
why it matters: Use territories to test whether a wall motion abnormality makes coronary sense. A defect confined to one territory suggests coronary disease; one that crosses territories suggests a nonischemic cause, a wraparound LAD or multivessel disease. Trap: the inferolateral wall was formerly called the posterior wall, and older questions may use posterior. Trap two: an inferior infarct with RV dysfunction warns of RV infarction, in which nitrates and diuretics can drop preload dangerously. Learn the overlap segments so you do not overcommit to a single artery.
on the registry: Expect questions asking which artery is likely occluded given a wall motion description in a particular view.
checkpoint: Anterior plus anteroseptum plus apex is LAD; inferior is RCA; lateral is circumflex

title: Mechanical Complications of MI
front clue: Days three to five: septal rupture, papillary rupture, free wall rupture
core concept: Mechanical complications of myocardial infarction are less common in the reperfusion era but remain life threatening and usually appear within the first week, often around days 3 to 5. Ventricular septal rupture occurs in anterior infarcts, typically apical, and in inferior infarcts, typically basal inferoseptal and often more complex and serpiginous. Color shows a left to right systolic jet across the septum with RV volume and pressure overload, and a new holosystolic murmur. Papillary muscle rupture causes acute severe MR; the posteromedial muscle is involved far more often because of its single blood supply from the PDA. The flail head may be seen prolapsing into the LA, and the LA may be small because the MR is acute. Free wall rupture usually causes sudden hemopericardium, tamponade and death; contained rupture forms a pseudoaneurysm. Other complications include LV thrombus at an akinetic apex, true aneurysm, pericardial effusion and pericarditis, including Dressler syndrome, RV infarction and dynamic LVOT obstruction from compensatory basal hyperkinesis.
why it matters: The clinical clue is sudden deterioration with a new murmur after an infarct. On echo, distinguish septal rupture from papillary rupture by the location of the high-velocity jet: across the septum into the RV versus into the LA. Trap: acute severe MR may look less dramatic by color because LA pressure rises quickly and the jet is brief and low velocity. Trap two: a new pericardial effusion after infarction, especially with echogenic clot, raises concern for free wall rupture. Posteromedial papillary rupture with an inferior infarct is the most common exam pairing.
on the registry: Expect questions on the timing of complications, which papillary muscle ruptures, septal rupture location and signs of free wall rupture.
checkpoint: Posteromedial papillary rupture: inferior MI, single PDA supply

title: LV Aneurysm vs Pseudoaneurysm
front clue: Wide neck and all three layers: true; narrow neck and only pericardium: false
core concept: A true LV aneurysm is a thinned, scarred segment of full-thickness myocardium that bulges outward in both systole and diastole with dyskinetic or akinetic motion. It most often follows an LAD infarct and involves the apex or anterior wall. Its neck is wide, about as wide as the aneurysm itself, and the wall contains myocardium. Complications include thrombus within the aneurysm, ventricular arrhythmias and heart failure, but rupture is rare. A pseudoaneurysm is a contained rupture of the LV free wall, walled off by adherent pericardium and thrombus without myocardium. It occurs more often after inferior or inferolateral infarcts, or after surgery or trauma. It has a narrow neck, with a neck to maximal diameter ratio usually under about 0.5, an abrupt transition from normal myocardium, and to-and-fro color flow through the neck, systolic into the sac and diastolic back. Pseudoaneurysms have a high risk of rupture and require urgent surgery. Contrast echo, CT or cardiac MRI can help when the distinction is unclear.
why it matters: The distinction changes management from elective to emergency, so the exam focuses on morphology. Neck width relative to the sac is the single most useful clue. Trap: a pseudoaneurysm can contain a lot of thrombus and look solid, so search for the narrow communication with color Doppler and pulsed Doppler. Trap two: a true aneurysm shows the wall tapering gradually from normal myocardium, while a pseudoaneurysm shows an abrupt break. Location helps but is not definitive: apical suggests true aneurysm, while inferior or inferolateral raises concern for a pseudoaneurysm.
on the registry: Expect questions on neck width, wall composition, typical location, color flow pattern and rupture risk.
checkpoint: Narrow neck under half the sac width means pseudoaneurysm

title: Stress Echocardiography
front clue: New or worse wall motion at peak stress means ischemia; biphasic response means viable
core concept: Stress echo compares wall motion at rest and during stress, using exercise or dobutamine. The target heart rate is at least 85 percent of age-predicted maximum, calculated as 220 minus age. Treadmill images must be acquired immediately after exercise, ideally within about 60 to 90 seconds, because wall motion recovers quickly; supine bicycle allows imaging during exercise. Dobutamine is infused in stages, typically from 5 or 10 to 40 mcg/kg/min, with atropine added if needed to reach target heart rate. Normal response is increased thickening and a smaller, hyperdynamic cavity. Ischemia is a new or worsening wall motion abnormality, LV cavity dilation or reduced global function at peak. A fixed resting abnormality that does not change suggests scar. A biphasic response, improvement at low dose and deterioration at high dose, indicates viable but ischemic myocardium, the strongest predictor of recovery after revascularization. Low-dose dobutamine is also used for low-flow, low-gradient AS. Stopping criteria include target heart rate, significant arrhythmia, hypotension, severe hypertension and new extensive wall motion abnormality.
why it matters: The core logic is supply and demand: stress increases demand, and a narrowed artery cannot increase supply, so the segment it feeds fails. Trap: delayed post-exercise imaging misses ischemia because the segment recovers. Trap two: a submaximal heart rate gives a nondiagnostic, not a normal, result. Beta blockers blunt the heart rate response. Left bundle branch block causes abnormal septal motion at rest that should not be called ischemia without thickening loss. For valve questions, contractile reserve on dobutamine is a stroke volume increase of 20 percent or more.
on the registry: Expect questions on target heart rate, the timing of post-exercise imaging, dobutamine dosing and how ischemia, scar and viability appear.
checkpoint: Target 85 percent of 220 minus age; image within about a minute

title: Pericardial vs Pleural Effusion
front clue: Descending aorta is the landmark: pericardial in front, pleural behind
core concept: The pericardium normally contains about 15 to 50 mL of fluid. A pericardial effusion appears as an echo-free space between the visceral and parietal pericardium, first seen posteriorly in dependent position and then circumferentially as it enlarges. Size is graded by end-diastolic separation: trivial when seen only in systole, small under 10 mm, moderate 10 to 20 mm and large over 20 mm. In parasternal long axis, pericardial fluid lies anterior to the descending thoracic aorta and tapers at the posterior AV groove, while left pleural fluid extends posterior to the descending aorta and does not stop at the AV groove. Pericardial fluid rarely collects behind the LA because the pericardial reflections around the pulmonary veins, forming the oblique sinus, limit it. An anterior echo-free space alone is often epicardial fat, which is slightly echogenic, moves with the heart and is most common in older, obese or diabetic patients. Fibrin strands, clot or loculation suggest an exudative, infectious, malignant or postoperative cause. Subcostal views help guide pericardiocentesis.
why it matters: The descending aorta landmark answers most exam questions, so find it on every parasternal long-axis view. Trap: an isolated anterior space is usually fat, not fluid; true effusion almost always appears posteriorly first. Trap two: pleural and pericardial effusions can coexist, giving a double layer around the aorta. Size does not equal hemodynamic effect; rapid accumulation of a small volume, such as after surgery or trauma, can cause tamponade, while a slowly growing large effusion may be tolerated. Loculated postoperative effusions can compress a single chamber and are easily missed, so scan from multiple windows.
on the registry: Expect questions on the descending aorta landmark, size categories, epicardial fat versus fluid and why fluid rarely collects behind the LA.
checkpoint: Pericardial anterior to descending aorta; pleural posterior to it

title: Cardiac Tamponade
front clue: RA collapse in systole, RV collapse in diastole, plethoric IVC, big respiratory swings
core concept: Cardiac tamponade occurs when pericardial pressure exceeds intracardiac pressure and impairs filling. It is a clinical diagnosis supported by echo. Findings include a pericardial effusion, often with a swinging heart in large effusions; right atrial collapse or inversion in late diastole and early systole, which is sensitive and becomes more specific when it lasts more than one third of the cardiac cycle; right ventricular free wall collapse in early diastole, which is more specific; a plethoric IVC with less than 50 percent inspiratory collapse, which is very sensitive; and exaggerated respiratory variation in inflow, with mitral E falling by more than about 25 to 30 percent with inspiration and tricuspid E varying by more than about 40 to 60 percent. The septum shifts toward the LV with inspiration, reflecting ventricular interdependence. Clinically, Beck triad, pulsus paradoxus over 10 mmHg and electrical alternans on ECG, which corresponds to the swinging heart, are classic. LA collapse can occur with loculated posterior or postoperative effusions.
why it matters: Reason in pressures: the lowest-pressure chambers collapse first, so the RA collapses before the RV, and the LA collapses only in unusual cases. Trap: RV hypertrophy or pulmonary hypertension raises right heart pressure and can prevent collapse, so tamponade may exist without RV collapse. Trap two: a normal, collapsing IVC makes tamponade very unlikely unless the patient is volume depleted, as in low-pressure tamponade. Mechanical ventilation reverses the normal respiratory pattern. Use M-mode with the cursor through the RV free wall to time collapse precisely to diastole.
on the registry: Expect questions on which chamber collapses first, which sign is most specific or sensitive, respiratory variation thresholds and clinical correlates.
checkpoint: RA collapse is early; RV diastolic collapse is specific; plethoric IVC is sensitive

title: Constrictive Pericarditis
front clue: Septal bounce, preserved e' and annulus reversus inside a rigid shell
core concept: Constrictive pericarditis is a rigid, often thickened or calcified pericardium that limits total cardiac volume. Causes include prior cardiac surgery, radiation, viral or idiopathic pericarditis, tuberculosis in endemic regions, and connective tissue disease. Echo features include a thickened, bright pericardium, a respirophasic septal shift or septal bounce, a dilated IVC with little collapse, and exaggerated respiratory variation in mitral inflow, with E decreasing by about 25 percent or more on inspiration. Filling is restrictive with a tall E and short deceleration time. Tissue Doppler e' is preserved or even increased, often with medial e' above about 8 cm/s, and annulus reversus, in which septal e' exceeds lateral e' because the lateral wall is tethered by the pericardium. Hepatic vein flow shows prominent diastolic flow reversal in expiration. The Mayo criteria combine septal shift, medial e' of 9 cm/s or more and expiratory hepatic vein diastolic reversal. Pericardial thickness is better measured with CT or MRI.
why it matters: Constriction versus restriction is a perennial exam topic. In constriction the myocardium is normal, so longitudinal tissue velocities are preserved, and the pericardium forces the ventricles to compete, so respiratory variation and septal shift are exaggerated. In restriction, the muscle is stiff, e' is low and respiratory variation is minimal. Trap: hepatic vein reversal timing differs, expiratory in constriction and inspiratory in restriction. Trap two: a normal-thickness pericardium does not exclude constriction. Effusive-constrictive pericarditis persists after drainage of an effusion and should be suspected when filling pressures stay high after pericardiocentesis.
on the registry: Expect questions comparing constriction with restriction, annulus reversus, hepatic vein reversal timing and respiratory variation thresholds.
checkpoint: Constriction: normal muscle, normal e', wild respiratory swings

title: Cardiac Myxoma
front clue: Left atrial mass on a stalk at the fossa ovalis that plops through the mitral valve
core concept: Myxoma is the most common primary benign cardiac tumor in adults, typically presenting in middle-aged women. About 75 percent arise in the left atrium and most of the rest in the right atrium; ventricular myxomas are rare. The tumor is usually attached by a narrow stalk to the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis. It is a mobile, gelatinous, heterogeneous mass that may contain lucent areas or calcification, and it often prolapses through the mitral valve in diastole. This can obstruct inflow and mimic mitral stenosis, with an increased diastolic gradient, and on M-mode a mass of echoes fills the space behind the anterior mitral leaflet in diastole. Patients may have dyspnea, syncope, embolism and constitutional symptoms, and auscultation may reveal a tumor plop. Most cases are sporadic; familial myxomas occur in Carney complex, often multiple and in unusual locations, in younger patients. Papillary fibroelastoma, the most common valvular tumor, is a small frond-like mass on the valve, usually the aortic.
why it matters: Location and attachment are the keys: a mobile LA mass attached to the septum is myxoma until proven otherwise, while a mass in the LA appendage of a patient with atrial fibrillation or mitral stenosis is more likely thrombus. Trap: the diastolic gradient from a prolapsing myxoma mimics MS, but the leaflets are thin and the commissures are not fused. Trap two: although myxoma is the most common primary benign tumor, metastases are far more common than any primary cardiac tumor. Embolic risk is substantial with friable villous myxomas, so surgery is not delayed.
on the registry: Expect questions on myxoma location, attachment, M-mode appearance, clinical presentation and how it differs from thrombus.
checkpoint: Myxoma: LA, septal stalk, fossa ovalis, diastolic prolapse

title: Thrombus & Metastatic Tumors
front clue: Thrombus lives where blood is slow; metastases outnumber primary tumors
core concept: Intracardiac thrombus forms where flow is stagnant. LA appendage thrombus is associated with atrial fibrillation, mitral stenosis and enlarged atria; it is best excluded with TEE, which also shows spontaneous echo contrast (smoke) and low appendage emptying velocities, often under about 20 cm/s. LV thrombus forms at akinetic or aneurysmal segments, most often the apex after an anterior infarct or in dilated cardiomyopathy; it appears as an echodense mass with a distinct margin from the endocardium, and contrast echo improves detection. Right heart thrombi include thrombi in transit from the venous system, which are serpiginous and highly mobile, and catheter-related thrombi. Metastatic tumors are about 20 to 40 times more common than primary cardiac tumors. Common sources are lung and breast cancer, lymphoma and leukemia; melanoma has a particularly high rate of cardiac involvement. Spread is by direct extension, lymphatics, blood or the venous route, such as renal cell carcinoma or hepatocellular carcinoma growing up the IVC into the right atrium. Pericardial metastasis often presents as a malignant effusion.
why it matters: Context drives the diagnosis. A mass in an akinetic apex is thrombus, a mobile septal mass is myxoma, and a mass growing from the IVC in a patient with a renal tumor is tumor extension. Trap: near-field clutter and apical trabeculations can mimic an apical thrombus; use a higher frequency, change the focus and depth or give contrast. A thrombus shows no perfusion with contrast, while vascular tumors enhance. Thrombi in transit across a PFO can cause paradoxical embolism and are an emergency. Smoke in the appendage indicates high thrombotic risk even without a discrete clot.
on the registry: Expect questions on where thrombi form, how contrast helps, which test excludes appendage thrombus and the most common cardiac tumor overall.
checkpoint: Most common cardiac tumor overall: metastasis

title: Normal Variants & Pseudomasses
front clue: Chiari network waves, Eustachian valve guards the IVC, the coumadin ridge is not a clot
core concept: Several normal structures mimic pathology. In the right atrium, the Eustachian valve is a ridge at the IVC-RA junction, a remnant of the fetal valve that directed IVC blood toward the foramen ovale. The Chiari network is a fenestrated, mobile, net-like remnant of the sinus venosus valves, attached near the IVC and coronary sinus, found in about 2 percent of people and associated with PFO and atrial septal aneurysm. The crista terminalis is a muscular ridge on the posterolateral RA wall. In the RV, the moderator band runs from the septum to the anterior free wall and carries part of the right bundle branch. In the LA, the coumadin (warfarin) ridge separates the LA appendage from the left upper pulmonary vein, and the appendage contains pectinate muscles that mimic small thrombi. Lipomatous hypertrophy of the interatrial septum is fatty thickening that spares the fossa ovalis, giving a dumbbell shape. Other variants include LV false tendons, Lambl excrescences and nodules of Arantius on the aortic cusps.
why it matters: These variants are tested because mistaking them for thrombus, tumor or vegetation leads to unnecessary procedures. Reason by location and texture: each variant appears in a typical place with a characteristic shape. Trap: a Chiari network is highly mobile and can look like a vegetation or thrombus, but it is thin, filamentous and attached near the IVC orifice. Trap two: lipomatous septal hypertrophy spares the fossa ovalis, while a myxoma typically attaches there. Pectinate muscles are multiple, parallel and fixed to the appendage wall, while thrombus is a discrete mass, often with surrounding smoke.
on the registry: Expect questions on identifying a described normal structure by location and on distinguishing variants from thrombus, tumor or vegetation.
checkpoint: Eustachian at the IVC, Chiari a mobile net, coumadin ridge by the left upper pulmonary vein

title: Atrial Septal Defects
front clue: Secundum in the middle, primum low, sinus venosus high near the SVC
core concept: Atrial septal defects are among the most common congenital lesions first found in adults. Secundum ASD, about 70 to 75 percent, is a defect at the fossa ovalis in the mid septum. Primum ASD, about 15 to 20 percent, sits in the lower septum next to the AV valves, is associated with a cleft anterior mitral leaflet and Down syndrome, and shows AV valves at the same level. Sinus venosus ASD, about 5 to 10 percent, usually lies superiorly near the SVC entry and is associated with partial anomalous pulmonary venous return of the right upper pulmonary vein. Coronary sinus (unroofed) ASD is rare and often associated with a persistent left SVC. A left to right shunt causes RV and RA volume overload, paradoxical septal motion and diastolic septal flattening. Shunt size is estimated by Qp:Qs, the ratio of RVOT to LVOT stroke volume; a ratio of 1.5 or more is generally considered significant. A PFO, a flap-like opening, is best shown with agitated saline.
why it matters: Location determines associations and treatment: only secundum defects with adequate rims are suitable for percutaneous device closure, while primum and sinus venosus defects need surgery. Trap: dropout in the thin fossa ovalis in apical views creates false defects; confirm in subcostal views with color and PW Doppler. Trap two: sinus venosus defects are easily missed on TTE, so unexplained RV dilation should prompt TEE or cardiac MRI. Low-velocity left to right flow is easily confused with SVC or IVC inflow along the septum. With Eisenmenger physiology, the shunt reverses and RV dilation is joined by severe pulmonary hypertension.
on the registry: Expect questions on ASD types and their associations, signs of RV volume overload, Qp:Qs and which defects are closed percutaneously.
checkpoint: Secundum is most common; primum pairs with cleft mitral; sinus venosus pairs with anomalous veins

title: VSD & PDA
front clue: Both shunts load the left heart; the VSD jet is systolic, the PDA flow is continuous
core concept: Ventricular septal defects are classified as perimembranous, the most common type in adults at about 70 to 80 percent, located just below the aortic valve near the septal tricuspid leaflet; muscular, often small and multiple; inlet, part of the AV canal spectrum; and outlet or supracristal, just below the pulmonic valve, which can cause aortic cusp prolapse and AR. A restrictive VSD has a high-velocity systolic jet, typically 4 to 5 m/s, and RVSP can be estimated as systolic blood pressure minus 4 times the VSD velocity squared. A patent ductus arteriosus connects the proximal descending aorta, just distal to the left subclavian artery, to the main or proximal left pulmonary artery. In the parasternal short-axis or high parasternal view, it produces continuous flow into the pulmonary artery that peaks in late systole. Both VSD and PDA volume load the LA and LV, while the RV is loaded mainly by pressure if pulmonary hypertension develops. Large unrepaired shunts can lead to Eisenmenger syndrome with shunt reversal.
why it matters: The chamber that dilates tells you where the extra volume goes. An ASD dilates the right heart, while a VSD or PDA dilates the left heart, because the extra blood returns through the lungs to the LA and LV. Trap: a high VSD velocity is good news, meaning the RV pressure is low and the defect restrictive; a low-velocity VSD jet suggests elevated RV pressure. Trap two: a PDA jet can be confused with PR or coronary flow in the pulmonary artery, but PDA flow is continuous and directed toward the pulmonic valve. Supracristal VSDs need monitoring for progressive AR.
on the registry: Expect questions on VSD types, RVSP from the VSD gradient, which chambers dilate and the continuous PDA flow pattern.
checkpoint: RVSP = systolic BP minus 4 x VSD velocity squared

title: Coarctation of the Aorta
front clue: Sawtooth descending aorta signal with a diastolic tail, and weak flow below
core concept: Coarctation is a narrowing of the descending thoracic aorta, usually juxtaductal, just distal to the left subclavian artery. It is associated with a bicuspid aortic valve in about half of cases, with Turner syndrome, and with intracranial aneurysms. Adults may present with upper extremity hypertension, a blood pressure gradient between arms and legs, weak femoral pulses and rib notching on chest radiograph from collateral vessels. Echo uses the suprasternal notch view, where 2D may show a shelf-like narrowing and color shows flow acceleration. CW Doppler through the descending aorta shows a high systolic velocity, and in significant coarctation a persistent forward diastolic tail, the sawtooth pattern, reflecting a continuing pressure gradient in diastole. Because the proximal velocity is often elevated, the expanded Bernoulli equation may be needed. Subcostal PW in the abdominal aorta shows low-velocity, blunted systolic flow with a delayed upstroke and continuous diastolic forward flow. LV hypertrophy is common. After repair, patients are monitored for recoarctation, aneurysm at the repair site and persistent hypertension.
why it matters: The diastolic tail matters more than peak velocity, because a peak gradient can be high in mild narrowing, while continuous diastolic flow means the obstruction is hemodynamically significant. Trap: well-developed collaterals can reduce the measured gradient despite severe narrowing, so a low gradient does not exclude severe coarctation. Trap two: blunted abdominal aortic flow with diastolic forward flow is an indirect clue when the suprasternal window is poor. Always look for coarctation in a young hypertensive patient or one with a bicuspid valve. CT or MRI is used for anatomy.
on the registry: Expect questions on location, associated lesions, the diastolic tail on CW Doppler and abdominal aortic flow patterns.
checkpoint: Diastolic tail on CW means significant coarctation

title: Ebstein Anomaly
front clue: Septal leaflet slides toward the apex, atrializing the RV
core concept: Ebstein anomaly is a congenital malformation of the tricuspid valve in which the septal and posterior (inferior) leaflets are displaced apically from the annulus, and the anterior leaflet is large, redundant and sail-like. The portion of the RV above the displaced leaflets becomes functionally part of the RA, the atrialized RV, leaving a smaller functional RV. In the apical four-chamber view, the key measurement is the distance between the mitral and tricuspid septal leaflet insertions; in adults an apical displacement of 8 mm/m2 of body surface area or more is diagnostic. Tricuspid regurgitation is common and can be severe, and the RA and atrialized RV are often massively dilated. Associated findings include an ASD or PFO in most patients, which can allow right to left shunting and cyanosis, accessory pathways such as Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, and occasionally LV noncompaction. Maternal lithium exposure is a classically cited association. Surgical repair, such as the cone procedure, reconstructs the valve.
why it matters: The key is that the normal tricuspid septal insertion is only slightly more apical than the mitral, so the measurement must be indexed and taken carefully in a true four-chamber view. Trap: severe TR from other causes dilates the RA and RV but does not displace leaflets. Trap two: the TR jet in Ebstein originates deep in the RV body, not at the anatomic annulus, so align color and CW from the true coaptation point. Look for an atrial shunt with agitated saline, because paradoxical embolism and cyanosis can result. Arrhythmias are a common adult presentation.
on the registry: Expect questions on which leaflets are displaced, the indexed displacement criterion, atrialized RV and associated lesions.
checkpoint: Displacement of 8 mm/m2 or more confirms Ebstein

title: Repaired Tetralogy of Fallot
front clue: Four defects fixed in childhood, chronic pulmonic regurgitation in adulthood
core concept: Tetralogy of Fallot comprises a VSD, an overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction (infundibular and often valvular pulmonic stenosis) and RV hypertrophy, all resulting from anterior deviation of the outlet septum. It is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease. Most adults have had surgical repair with VSD patch closure and relief of RVOT obstruction, often with a transannular patch that leaves the pulmonic valve incompetent. The dominant long-term problem is chronic pulmonic regurgitation, which progressively dilates the RV and can cause RV dysfunction, arrhythmias and sudden death. Echo assesses RV size and function, PR severity, residual RVOT or branch pulmonary artery stenosis, residual VSD patch leaks, TR, RVSP, aortic root dilation, AR and LV function. Severe PR shows a broad jet, a short dense CW signal ending early in diastole and diastolic flow reversal in the branch pulmonary arteries. Cardiac MRI is the reference for RV volumes and guides the timing of pulmonary valve replacement, increasingly done percutaneously.
why it matters: Free PR is easy to underestimate on echo because the flow is laminar and low velocity, with little color turbulence, so focus on the CW signal shape and RV size. A short PR signal ending well before the next systole means the RV and PA pressures equalize early. Trap: a high RVSP after repair suggests residual RVOT or branch PA stenosis rather than pulmonary vascular disease. Trap two: the overriding aorta can dilate, leading to AR. Restrictive RV physiology, with antegrade diastolic PA flow during atrial contraction, is an important finding in some patients.
on the registry: Expect questions on the four components, the transannular patch and PR, and echo targets on follow-up.
checkpoint: Tetralogy: VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, RVH

title: Marfan Syndrome & Aortic Root Dilation
front clue: Sinuses balloon and the sinotubular junction disappears: a flask-shaped root
core concept: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by FBN1 (fibrillin-1) mutations. The cardinal cardiovascular finding is dilation of the aortic root, maximal at the sinuses of Valsalva, with effacement of the sinotubular junction, giving a pear or flask shape. Other findings include mitral valve prolapse with myxomatous leaflets, MR and AR from annular dilation. The aorta is measured in the parasternal long-axis view at the annulus, sinuses of Valsalva, sinotubular junction and proximal ascending aorta, perpendicular to the long axis. ASE recommends measuring the annulus inner edge to inner edge in mid-systole, and the other levels at end-diastole using the leading edge to leading edge convention; other conventions exist, so consistency across serial studies matters. Measurements are compared with body size, age and sex using z-scores. In Marfan syndrome, elective surgery is generally considered at a root diameter of about 5.0 cm, or lower with rapid growth or a family history of dissection. Other causes of root dilation include bicuspid aortopathy, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, hypertension and aging.
why it matters: The risk is dissection, which correlates with size and growth rate, so serial measurements must be done the same way at the same levels. Trap: an oblique cut underestimates the true diameter; obtain the largest perpendicular diameter. Trap two: in Marfan syndrome, dilation starts at the sinuses, while in hypertension and aging the ascending aorta above the junction is more often enlarged. Annular dilation causes central AR, which worsens as the root grows. Loeys-Dietz syndrome causes dissection at smaller diameters, so surgical thresholds are lower.
on the registry: Expect questions on where dilation begins, measurement levels and conventions, associated valve disease and surgical thresholds.
checkpoint: Marfan dilates the sinuses first and erases the sinotubular junction

title: Aortic Dissection
front clue: A mobile intimal flap splits true from false lumen; type A goes to surgery
core concept: Aortic dissection is a tear in the intima that allows blood to enter the media, creating a true lumen and a false lumen separated by a mobile intimal flap. Hypertension is the most common risk factor; others include Marfan and other connective tissue syndromes, bicuspid aortic valve, cocaine and pregnancy. The Stanford classification is type A, involving the ascending aorta regardless of origin, a surgical emergency, and type B, confined to the aorta distal to the left subclavian artery, often managed medically. DeBakey type I involves the ascending aorta and extends beyond it, type II is confined to the ascending aorta, and type III is limited to the descending aorta. On echo, the true lumen is usually smaller, expands in systole and has faster flow, while the false lumen is larger with slower flow, spontaneous echo contrast or thrombus. Complications seen on echo include acute AR, pericardial effusion and tamponade, coronary involvement with a wall motion abnormality, often inferior from the RCA, and branch vessel malperfusion.
why it matters: TTE can confirm a type A dissection when a flap is seen in the root, but a normal TTE does not exclude it, so CT or TEE follows. Trap: reverberation and side lobe artifacts in the ascending aorta mimic flaps; a true flap moves independently, appears in multiple views and has distinct flow on each side with color. Trap two: a new pericardial effusion in suspected type A dissection signals impending rupture and tamponade. Intramural hematoma and penetrating ulcer are related acute aortic syndromes. TEE has a blind spot in the distal ascending aorta behind the trachea.
on the registry: Expect questions on the Stanford and DeBakey classifications, true versus false lumen features, complications and artifact mimics.
checkpoint: Stanford A: ascending, surgical; Stanford B: descending only, often medical

title: Doppler Modes in Echo
front clue: PW knows where but aliases; CW handles speed but cannot tell where
core concept: Doppler measures blood velocity from the frequency shift: shift equals 2 times transmitted frequency times velocity times the cosine of the angle, divided by propagation speed. In echo, the beam is aligned as parallel to flow as possible and no angle correction is used, because errors over about 20 degrees significantly underestimate velocity. Pulsed wave Doppler uses one crystal to transmit and receive from a chosen depth, giving range resolution, but it aliases when the shift exceeds the Nyquist limit, half the PRF. Continuous wave Doppler uses separate transmitting and receiving elements and measures very high velocities without aliasing, but it has range ambiguity, recording the highest velocity anywhere along the beam; it is used for AS, MR, TR, AR and VSD jets. High PRF Doppler uses multiple sample volumes to raise the measurable velocity at the cost of range ambiguity. Color Doppler uses autocorrelation to show mean velocity and direction, conventionally red toward and blue away from the transducer, with variance showing turbulence.
why it matters: Aliasing is the classic question. To reduce it, raise the scale or PRF, shift the baseline, use a lower transmit frequency, reduce depth or switch to CW Doppler. Trap: increasing the transducer frequency makes aliasing worse because the shift increases. Trap two: CW cannot localize a jet, so a high velocity could be AS, MR or something else along the line; use timing, shape and the 2D image to identify it. Color jets depend on gain, Nyquist limit and frame rate; a lower Nyquist limit makes jets look larger, so standard settings around 50 to 70 cm/s are used for regurgitation.
on the registry: Expect questions on which Doppler mode suits a measurement, the Nyquist limit, ways to eliminate aliasing and angle effects.
checkpoint: Nyquist limit = PRF / 2

title: M-Mode & Tissue Doppler
front clue: M-mode is motion over time at one line; tissue Doppler hears the slow, loud myocardium
core concept: M-mode displays the motion of structures along a single scan line over time, with very high temporal resolution because thousands of pulses per second are sent down one line. It is ideal for timing events and fast motion: valve opening and closing, SAM, aortic valve notching in HCM, mitral fluttering in AR, RV collapse in tamponade, and TAPSE. Color M-mode of mitral inflow measures flow propagation velocity, with values above about 50 cm/s considered normal. Tissue Doppler imaging measures myocardial velocities, which are low velocity and high amplitude, the opposite of blood; the wall filter and gain are reduced to display them. PW tissue Doppler at the mitral annulus records s', e' and a'. Normal e' is at least about 7 cm/s at the septal and 10 cm/s at the lateral annulus. Strain and strain rate describe deformation; global longitudinal strain more negative than about -18 percent is generally normal.
why it matters: M-mode is a timing tool; when a question asks about rapid events or precise timing, it is often the answer. Trap: an oblique M-mode cursor overestimates LV dimensions, so 2D linear measurements are now preferred. Tissue Doppler, like all Doppler, is angle dependent, so annular velocities are taken from apical views where motion is parallel to the beam. Strain from speckle tracking is relatively angle independent but vendor dependent, so serial studies should use the same platform. Remember that tissue Doppler filters are the reverse of blood flow Doppler: reject low amplitude, keep low velocity.
on the registry: Expect questions on M-mode temporal resolution and uses, tissue Doppler signal characteristics and filter settings, and normal e' values.
checkpoint: Tissue Doppler: low velocity, high amplitude

title: Harmonics, Artifacts & ALARA
front clue: Harmonics clean the picture, artifacts fake structures, ALARA keeps exposure low
core concept: Tissue harmonic imaging receives echoes at twice the transmitted frequency, which are generated as sound propagates nonlinearly through tissue. Harmonics form mostly in the central beam and deeper tissue, so they reduce near-field clutter, side lobe and reverberation artifacts, improving endocardial border definition, particularly in difficult patients. Pulse inversion is a common method. A drawback is that valves and walls look thicker. Common echo artifacts include reverberation, parallel lines behind strong reflectors such as prosthetic valves or calcium; acoustic shadowing behind mechanical valves and calcification; side lobe and grating lobe artifacts, which place false echoes in the aortic root or LA; mirror image artifacts, duplicating structures across a strong reflector such as the pericardium; refraction, causing side-by-side duplication; near-field clutter mimicking apical thrombus; and range ambiguity. Safety follows ALARA: as low as reasonably achievable output and exposure time. The mechanical index reflects cavitation risk, with an FDA limit of 1.9 for most diagnostic applications, and the thermal index reflects heating. TEE probes monitor tip temperature.
why it matters: Artifacts are tested by asking how to tell a real structure from a false one. Real structures appear in more than one view, have anatomic attachments and move independently; artifacts often sit at fixed multiples of a reflector's depth or move with it. Trap: harmonics improve borders but thicken valves, so do not diagnose valve thickening from harmonic images alone. Trap two: increasing gain does not fix shadowing; change the window. For ALARA, reduce output power before increasing receiver gain, and freeze the image when not scanning. Low MI settings are used for contrast to avoid bubble destruction.
on the registry: Expect questions on how harmonics are generated, which artifacts they reduce, recognizing echo artifacts and the meaning of MI and TI.
checkpoint: Real structures appear in two views; artifacts usually do not
ai_review_note: whyLock (low): The ALARA rule is usually taught as raising receiver gain before raising output power; the original wording can be read the wrong way.

title: Contrast & Agitated Saline
front clue: Commercial microbubbles cross the lungs; agitated saline bubbles do not
core concept: Ultrasound enhancing agents are gas-filled microspheres, such as perflutren lipid or protein microspheres and sulfur hexafluoride microbubbles, small enough to pass through the pulmonary capillaries and opacify the left heart. ASE recommends contrast when two or more contiguous LV segments are not visualized, to improve EF and wall motion assessment, detect LV thrombus, confirm apical HCM, LV noncompaction or aneurysm and assess masses. Imaging uses a low mechanical index, about 0.2 or less, to avoid destroying bubbles. Agitated saline, mixed with a small amount of air and sometimes blood, produces larger bubbles that are filtered by the lungs, so it normally opacifies only the right heart. It is used to detect intracardiac shunts such as PFO and ASD, often with Valsalva release or cough, and to enhance TR Doppler signals. Bubbles in the left heart within about three cardiac cycles suggest an intracardiac shunt, while later appearance suggests an intrapulmonary shunt. Left arm injection with early coronary sinus opacification indicates a persistent left SVC.
why it matters: Know which agent does what: commercial contrast is for the left heart and endocardial borders, agitated saline for shunts and the right heart. Trap: an inadequate Valsalva or high LA pressure can mask a PFO, so release the strain once the RA is opacified to transiently raise RA pressure above LA pressure. Trap two: the timing of bubbles in the left heart distinguishes intracardiac from intrapulmonary shunting. High MI destroys bubbles and causes apical swirling, so lower the MI; swirling can also mean too little agent, while too much agent causes far-field (basal) attenuation shadowing, so adjust the infusion rate. Monitor patients during and after commercial agent administration.
on the registry: Expect questions on contrast indications, low MI imaging, agitated saline timing for shunts, Valsalva technique and persistent left SVC.
checkpoint: Bubbles left within three beats: intracardiac shunt

title: TEE Indications & Views
front clue: From the esophagus, the LA is closest; look for appendage clot, vegetations and dissection
core concept: Transesophageal echo places a high-frequency transducer in the esophagus and stomach directly behind the heart, avoiding lung and chest wall, so posterior structures such as the LA, LA appendage, mitral valve, interatrial septum and descending aorta are seen in high resolution. Common indications are excluding LA appendage thrombus before cardioversion or ablation, suspected endocarditis and abscess, prosthetic valve dysfunction, aortic dissection, cardioembolic stroke and PFO evaluation, mitral valve repair planning, intraoperative monitoring and guidance of structural interventions. Contraindications include esophageal stricture, tumor, perforation, recent esophageal surgery and active upper GI bleeding. Standard views include the midesophageal four-chamber view at about 0 degrees, the mitral commissural view at about 60 degrees, the two-chamber view at about 90 degrees, often used for the LA appendage, and the long-axis view at about 120 to 140 degrees. The midesophageal aortic valve short axis is about 30 to 45 degrees, the bicaval view about 90 to 110 degrees, and transgastric views show the LV short axis and allow Doppler alignment for aortic valve gradients.
why it matters: TEE trades patient comfort and small risk for image quality, so the exam asks when it is worth it. Think posterior and small: appendage thrombus, small vegetations, prosthetic mitral regurgitation and abscesses. Trap: the distal ascending aorta and proximal arch form a blind spot because the air-filled trachea lies between the esophagus and aorta. Trap two: aortic valve gradients are often underestimated from midesophageal views; use deep transgastric views for alignment. Complications include sore throat, aspiration, esophageal injury, arrhythmias and methemoglobinemia from benzocaine spray. Patients fast and are monitored during sedation.
on the registry: Expect questions on TEE indications and contraindications, typical view angles, the tracheal blind spot and complications.
checkpoint: TEE blind spot: distal ascending aorta behind the trachea
